paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a mapping from one string to another, a task called transduction. Such mappings arise in natural language processing and computational biology. Earlier approaches described in the abstract use classification techniques. This work instead develops a general regression approach, making the prediction of an output sequence part of a regression framework.

The method separates learning into two stages. First, it estimates regression coefficients through a reformulation of kernel dependency estimation. Second, it computes the corresponding pre-image: the output string associated with those coefficients. This second step connects the numerical representation produced by regression to the structured answer the application actually needs.

The authors contribute both a cleaner formulation for estimating the coefficients and an efficient algorithm for recovering output sequences. Together, these developments extend the applicability of kernel dependency estimation to sequence outputs. A series of experiments illustrates the method and supports its effectiveness for learning transductions, establishing regression as a workable approach to this string-to-string prediction problem.
icml-2005-a-general-regression-technique.tldr: A two-stage regression method learns string-to-string mappings by estimating coefficients and efficiently recovering an output sequence.

paragraphs: The paper approaches learning as a search for functions that closely track the observed data. The data are treated as observations generated by an unknown function, and the goal is to build an approximation of that function. Highly correlated candidate functions provide useful pieces from which that approximation can be assembled.

The main contribution is a search algorithm for finding these correlated functions for an arbitrary dataset. Learning a Fourier representation is a special case of the approach, so the proposed framework extends beyond that particular form of representation. Its central idea is to identify useful component functions through their relationship with the data and then combine them.

The empirical results address both the search and the resulting approximation. On the typical real-world problems studied, the most highly correlated functions are found very quickly, and combinations of those functions approximate the unknown function well. These findings support the practical value of the search strategy, while the reported speed remains an empirical observation about the studied problems.
icml-2005-a-practical-generalization-of-.tldr: A search algorithm finds functions strongly correlated with data and combines them into useful approximations, generalizing Fourier-based learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies dimensionality reduction when observations come with information about the actions linking them. It assumes that the data form a sequence and that adjacent observations have associated action labels, as could happen when a mobile robot records its experience. The desired representation must therefore capture more than a compact description of individual observations.

The proposed representation is low-dimensional and makes actions correspond to simple transformations. This connects the geometry of the representation to how the observed system changes under an action. The authors show that this version of dimensionality reduction can be formulated and solved as a semidefinite program, giving a concrete optimization approach to the combined requirements.

Evaluation takes place in a synthetic domain inspired by robotics. The resulting representations are qualitatively better, and the method also improves performance on a data prediction task. These findings support using action information to shape a representation when such labels are available. The evidence concerns the synthetic setting studied, rather than a demonstrated deployment on a physical robot.
icml-2005-action-respecting-embedding-20.tldr: Action respecting embedding learns compact representations in which labeled actions become simple transformations.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a clustering algorithm that uses the internal structure revealed by the data. It builds on a consistency method originally used for semi-supervised learning, which learns functions that vary smoothly with that structure. This gives the clustering procedure a way to account for relationships among observations when identifying useful groups.

The method also identifies representative examples and unusual observations. It detects both global outliers and outliers within individual classes, providing information beyond cluster membership alone. The abstract contrasts these capabilities with spectral clustering. An accompanying optimization framework estimates all learning parameters from the data, including how many clusters to use.

The learned cluster models can also assign previously unseen points without relearning the original clustering. This makes the model useful beyond the dataset on which it was first constructed. Experiments on several real-world problems produce encouraging results. Together, the contributions combine grouping, representative-example selection, outlier detection, and assignment of new observations within one clustering approach.
icml-2005-clustering-through-ranking-on-.tldr: A structure-aware clustering method identifies groups, representatives, and outliers while estimating its parameters and accommodating new points.

paragraphs: The paper develops a regression algorithm in the context of first-order learning, motivated by relational reinforcement learning. Existing approaches described in the abstract follow either a model-based or an instance-based strategy. Each has a characteristic drawback: model-based methods can approximate the target function too coarsely, while instance-based methods can require substantial computation.

The proposed algorithm combines the two strategies to draw on their strengths. It is incremental, so learning proceeds as examples become available. The design aims to retain computational efficiency while improving the quality of the predictions, addressing the tradeoff that arises when either strategy is used on its own.

The authors report that the combined method is computationally efficient and produces better predictions earlier in the learning experiment. The timing of that improvement matters because an incremental learner makes predictions while its experience is still accumulating. The stated contribution is therefore both a hybrid approach to first-order regression and evidence that the combination can improve early learning behavior.
icml-2005-combining-model-based-and-inst.tldr: An incremental first-order regression algorithm combines model-based and instance-based learning for efficient computation and better early predictions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a framework for studying supervised learning through reductions: transformations that let one learning task be handled using a solution to another. Its central example converts multiclass cost-sensitive classification into binary classification. In the original task, choosing different labels can incur different costs, so ordinary classification accuracy does not fully describe the objective.

The reduction comes with an explicit conditional guarantee. If the learned binary classifier has error at most epsilon, the resulting cost-sensitive classifier has cost at most twice epsilon times the expected sum of costs across all possible labels. This quantifies how error in the binary problem affects cost in the original problem.

The scope extends to supervised tasks with bounded loss and finitely many choices, because those tasks can be represented as cost-sensitive classification. Under this formulation, a binary classification oracle can be used to solve them. Experiments also show the new reduction outperforming existing multiclass cost-sensitive learning algorithms, providing empirical support alongside the theoretical error-to-cost relationship.
icml-2005-error-limiting-reductions-betw.tldr: A reduction converts cost-sensitive learning into binary classification with a bound linking binary error to the original task’s cost.

paragraphs: The paper studies ensemble classification using the mathematical framework of Monte Carlo stochastic algorithms. This perspective treats the ensemble’s behavior as something that can be analyzed probabilistically. The focus is on connecting theoretical predictions about ensemble accuracy with experimental observations and on comparing two approaches to constructing ensemble classifiers.

Within this framework, the authors describe a new ensemble classifier whose probability distribution of accuracy can be computed exactly. That distribution is the theoretical object under study: it characterizes possible accuracy outcomes probabilistically. Having an exactly computable distribution provides a concrete basis for checking whether observed experimental behavior agrees with the analysis.

The experimental program has two stated goals. One is to compare theoretical predictions with measured results; the other is to systematically compare Monte Carlo ensemble classification with bagging. The abstract establishes these comparisons as the paper’s purpose without naming a winning method. Its contribution centers on bringing an analytically tractable ensemble classifier into an experimental comparison with a familiar alternative.
icml-2005-experimental-comparison-betwee.tldr: The paper compares bagging with a Monte Carlo ensemble classifier whose accuracy distribution can be computed exactly.

paragraphs: The paper introduces FCNN, an algorithm that selects a smaller subset of training examples for nearest-neighbor classification. The selected subset is consistent with the training set, preserving the required training classifications under the nearest-neighbor decision rule. This addresses the practical question of how much training data a nearest-neighbor model needs to retain.

FCNN has several stated computational properties. Its result does not depend on the order of the training examples, and its worst-case running time grows subquadratically with training-set size. It also converges in few iterations. The algorithm is likely to select points near the decision boundary, concentrating the retained examples around locations where classification decisions change.

Experiments compare FCNN with leading competence-preservation methods on large, multidimensional training sets. FCNN performs better in learning speed, scaling behavior, and model size, while maintaining comparable prediction accuracy. These results support the method as a way to reduce the stored model and accelerate its construction without sacrificing comparable predictive performance in the reported comparisons.
icml-2005-fast-condensed-nearest-neighbo.tldr: FCNN efficiently selects a compact, training-consistent nearest-neighbor subset and achieves comparable prediction accuracy in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning in non-cooperative situations involving multiple agents. Its starting point is that there cannot be a globally optimal learning algorithm whose behavior is independent of its opponents. A useful decision framework must therefore account for the possibility that different opponents call for different strategies.

The proposed approach minimizes regret over a set of strategies designed for possible opponent models. These strategies provide alternative ways to act, each suited to a different view of the other agents. Regret minimization supplies a framework for deciding among those alternatives, making the available strategy set central to how the agent adapts its behavior.

The paper extends this framework with longer playing horizons and experts that continue learning while they play. The candidate strategies can thus evolve with experience, and decisions can account for a longer stretch of interaction. The authors state that these changes can overcome several shortcomings of earlier multi-agent learning approaches. The resulting proposal remains sensitive to opponents, consistent with the problem’s initial motivation.
icml-2005-hedged-learning-regret-minimiz.tldr: Hedged learning extends regret minimization with longer horizons and adaptive experts for interactions with different potential opponents.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction problems whose outputs are structured objects, such as strings, trees, or partitions. Existing approaches often extend classification methods to simple graphical structures where exact search and parameter estimation are feasible. More complicated output spaces frequently make those exact computations impractical, creating a central obstacle for learning and prediction.

The authors make approximate search part of the learning formulation itself. Their framework treats learning as an optimization of the search process used to produce structured outputs. This brings parameter learning and decoding into a shared approach, so the learning problem reflects the approximate procedure that will actually be used to find predictions.

The paper provides two parameter-update methods together with convergence theorems and bounds. It also reports empirical evidence that this integrated approach can outperform exact models while using less computation. The performance statement is a demonstrated possibility, rather than a universal ranking of approximate and exact methods. The broader contribution is a framework that directly incorporates computationally feasible search into structured prediction.
icml-2005-learning-as-search-optimizatio.tldr: A structured-prediction framework integrates learning with approximate search and can improve performance while reducing computation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to learn a Bayesian network’s structure when the goal is classification. Candidate structures need a score, but commonly used scores are not well suited to distinguishing classes. Class-conditional likelihood is more appropriate for that purpose, yet its inability to decompose makes it infeasible for large domains.

The authors introduce approximate conditional likelihood, or ACL, as a decomposable scoring function. The aim is to identify network structures useful for class discrimination while making the scoring problem more manageable. The method is evaluated through dynamic Bayesian networks, connecting the new structural score to the classification performance of the resulting models.

On simulated data, networks trained with ACL achieve classification performance competitive with networks trained using class-conditional likelihood. In a neuroscience application too large for that likelihood-based approach, ACL-trained networks outperform BDE-trained networks, Gaussian naïve Bayes networks, and support vector machines. These results support ACL as a practical scoring alternative that preserves useful class-discrimination behavior in the reported settings.
icml-2005-learning-class-discriminative-.tldr: A decomposable approximate conditional-likelihood score makes discriminative dynamic Bayesian network structure learning practical in larger domains.

paragraphs: The paper examines repeated general-sum games in which agents learn while interacting. It argues that focusing on immediate best responses or equilibria of a single round can lead to relatively low average payoffs. Looking instead at equilibria of the repeated interaction motivates a learner that considers both protection against poor outcomes and opportunities for mutually beneficial behavior.

The authors identify two desired properties. An agent should never learn a strategy whose average payoff falls below the game’s minimax value. It should also learn to cooperate or compromise when doing so is beneficial. The abstract states that no existing learning algorithm was known to possess both properties.

The proposed reinforcement learning algorithm, M-Qubed, addresses these goals with different kinds of evidence. The payoff-protection property is proved. Cooperation and compromise are observed empirically in self-play across a wide range of games. This distinction matters: the paper provides a formal guarantee for the first goal and experimental support, specifically in self-play, for the second.
icml-2005-learning-to-compete-compromise.tldr: M-Qubed guarantees minimax payoff protection and empirically learns beneficial cooperation or compromise in self-play.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how gradient descent can be used to learn a ranking function. The target is a function that supports ordering items, with internet search providing one of the application settings considered. The work brings together a training objective and a model for the function that determines the ranking.

The authors propose a simple probabilistic cost function and introduce RankNet as a neural-network implementation of the approach. The cost function supplies the quantity that learning seeks to improve, while the neural network represents the underlying ranking function. Gradient descent connects these components by adjusting the model in response to the training objective.

Testing covers both toy data and data from a commercial internet search engine. This places the proposed learning method in a simplified setting and an application-oriented setting. The abstract reports the presence of these tests without stating comparative outcomes. The central contribution is the probabilistic training formulation and its realization in RankNet, establishing a concrete neural-network approach to learning rankings.
icml-2005-learning-to-rank-using-gradien.tldr: RankNet uses a neural network and a probabilistic cost function to learn rankings through gradient descent.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a decision-tree learning algorithm for the original multi-instance learning setting. The authors emphasize that adapting a familiar tree learner requires care: earlier attempts either use a somewhat different setting or overlook difficulties that arise in the original formulation. Their goal is to address those difficulties while staying close to standard tree-learning algorithms.

The contribution lies in a small number of consequential changes to existing multi-instance tree-learning approaches. The authors motivate these differences with theoretical arguments, connecting the algorithm’s design to the requirements of the learning setting. This makes fidelity to the original problem formulation a central part of the method.

Experiments use both synthetic and real-life datasets. They confirm that the design differences have a beneficial effect and show the resulting system outperforming existing multi-instance decision-tree learners. The findings support the value of carefully adapting the learning procedure to the intended setting. The reported improvement concerns the evaluated tree learners, with theoretical motivation and empirical comparisons providing complementary support.
icml-2005-multi-instance-tree-learning-1.tldr: A carefully adapted decision-tree algorithm improves multi-instance learning while retaining the original problem setting.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an unsupervised method for jointly clustering several types of entities, such as documents, words, and authors. Its input is co-occurrence information describing pairwise interactions between entity types. The goal is to learn several related clusterings together, allowing those observed relationships to inform how each type is grouped.

The objective measures mutual information between pairs of cluster variables, rewarding groupings that retain informative relationships across types. The algorithm alternates top-down clustering for some variables with bottom-up clustering for others. A local optimization routine then corrects the clustering choices, providing an additional way to improve the joint objective.

The empirical study focuses on document clustering and examines two-way, three-way, and four-way versions across six real-world datasets, including 20 Newsgroups and the Enron email collection. The proposed algorithms consistently and significantly outperform earlier leading information-theoretic clustering methods in these experiments. The results support jointly exploiting multiple types of co-occurrence information for document clustering in the studied settings.
icml-2005-multi-way-distributional-clust.tldr: Multi-way distributional clustering jointly groups different entity types by preserving information in their pairwise co-occurrences.

paragraphs: The paper proposes two support-vector methods for ordinal regression, where the prediction categories have an order. Both approaches learn multiple thresholds that define parallel discriminant hyperplanes for the ordinal scales. The thresholds therefore organize the model’s decisions according to the ordering that the prediction task requires.

A central property is that both methods guarantee correctly ordered thresholds at the optimal solution. This ties the optimization result to the intended ordinal structure. The authors also state that the size of each optimization problem grows linearly with the number of training examples, an important distinction from the time needed to solve it.

To perform the optimization, the paper adapts the SMO algorithm. The adapted solver is described as very easy to implement, with computational scaling quadratic in the number of examples. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets support the usefulness of both approaches. Together, the contributions combine an ordering guarantee, a stated optimization size, and a practical procedure for fitting the proposed ordinal models.
icml-2005-new-approaches-to-support-vect.tldr: Two support-vector ordinal regression methods guarantee ordered thresholds at the optimum and use an adapted SMO solver.

paragraphs: The paper studies surf-height prediction with a decision-oriented goal: estimating whether the height will fall within a surfable range. A single most likely height does not directly express the probability of that event. Predicting the full distribution instead supplies information about the likelihood of values falling inside or outside ranges of interest.

The surf data studied have a distribution that differs substantially from a normal distribution, making this prediction problem harder. The authors address that feature using an ensemble of mixture density networks to predict a probability density function. This makes the distribution itself the model’s output and connects the prediction to the range-based question.

The evaluation finds the approach effective for the surf-height problem studied. The paper also describes a web application that presents the resulting predictions in a usable form. Its contribution therefore spans both distribution prediction and presentation: the learning method estimates uncertainty across possible heights, and the application makes those estimates available for interpreting surf conditions.
icml-2005-predicting-probability-distrib.tldr: An ensemble of mixture density networks predicts surf-height distributions to estimate the probability of surfable conditions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the use of low-rank matrix approximations to make kernel methods practical for large learning problems. Conventional decomposition procedures typically work independently of the prediction task. The authors identify this separation as a potential source of inefficiency: an approximation may be constructed without considering the information the learner is trying to predict.

Their algorithm incorporates side information, such as classification labels or regression responses, into the decomposition of the kernel matrix. This makes the approximation sensitive to the learning task. The computational scaling remains favorable: it is linear in the number of data points and quadratic in the chosen approximation rank, matching the stated scaling of incomplete Cholesky decomposition.

Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm produces decompositions with significantly smaller rank than incomplete Cholesky decomposition. That result matters because rank is a direct component of the method’s computational scaling. The work supports using prediction information during matrix approximation, with the reported simulations demonstrating more compact decompositions.
icml-2005-predictive-low-rank-decomposit.tldr: A task-aware kernel decomposition uses labels or responses to obtain smaller-rank approximations while retaining favorable computational scaling.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic approach to learning preferences using Gaussian processes and kernels. The learning signal consists of preference relations, and the aim is to represent those relations within a Bayesian model. This connects the observed preferences to a framework that supports probabilistic predictions and model selection.

A central contribution is a new likelihood function designed to capture preference relations. The likelihood supplies the connection between those observations and the Bayesian formulation. The authors also give a generalized version that applies to many multiclass problems, extending the scope of the approach beyond its initial preference-learning motivation.

Experiments compare the method with a constraint-classification approach on several benchmark datasets. The reported results support the algorithm’s usefulness. The contribution is thus a combination of a preference-specific probabilistic formulation and evidence that it works in benchmark comparisons. Its Bayesian treatment also provides the stated advantages for selecting models and expressing predictions probabilistically, making those capabilities part of the proposed learning approach.
icml-2005-preference-learning-with-gauss.tldr: A Gaussian-process preference learner introduces a likelihood for preference relations and supports Bayesian model selection and probabilistic prediction.

paragraphs: The paper explores how to recognize, generalize, and reproduce gestures from human demonstrations. Its goal is a representation that keeps the important aspects of a gesture while discarding variation associated with an individual person’s motion. This requires handling both the complexity of recorded movement and the sequential character of a gesture.

The first processing stage compares principal component analysis with independent component analysis. These methods are used to decorrelate and denoise the data and reduce its dimensionality, making subsequent processing tractable. The second stage uses continuous hidden Markov models to encode the motion probabilistically, capturing its sequence and intrinsic variability through stochastic state-based representations.

The method is validated with a humanoid robot reproducing a variety of gestures performed by a human demonstrator. This connects the learned representation to physical reproduction, one of the paper’s stated goals. The framework combines preprocessing for manageable motion data with probabilistic sequence modeling, and the robot demonstration provides evidence of its use for gesture reproduction.
icml-2005-recognition-and-reproduction-o.tldr: The framework combines dimensionality reduction with hidden Markov models to represent human gestures and reproduce them on a humanoid robot.

paragraphs: The paper studies inductive process modeling, which builds quantitative models of dynamical systems using background knowledge about possible component processes. Earlier methods tend to overfit the training data. Ensemble learning offers a possible response, but combining models can make the result harder for domain scientists to understand.

The proposed approach uses multiple learned models to guide the construction of a final model. It first induces process models from different samples of the training data. Those models then inform a final search over model structures. This uses information from repeated modeling efforts while addressing the comprehensibility concern that motivates the work.

Experiments with synthetic and natural data suggest that the method reduces error and lowers the chance of including unnecessary processes. These are complementary outcomes: the model can predict better while containing fewer unsupported components. The evidence is suggestive, as stated in the abstract. The contribution is a way to use sample-based variation in learned models to guide a final structural search.
icml-2005-reducing-overfitting-in-proces.tldr: Models learned from different data samples guide a final process-model search, with experiments suggesting less error and fewer unnecessary processes.

paragraphs: The paper extends Gaussian Process Temporal Difference learning, a Bayesian method for evaluating a reinforcement-learning policy. It addresses two issues that the earlier framework did not adequately handle: randomness in state transitions and the need to select actions and improve a policy. These extensions connect value estimation more closely to the broader learning problem.

The authors introduce a generative model for the value function based on its relationship with discounted return. From this model, they derive an online algorithm for learning the posterior moments of the value Gaussian process. This provides a sequential procedure for updating the Bayesian description of value as experience becomes available.

The paper also introduces GPSARSA, a SARSA-based extension of GPTD. GPSARSA supports action selection and gradual policy improvement without requiring a model of the world. The contribution therefore reaches beyond evaluating a fixed policy: it adds a way to use the Gaussian-process framework as part of choosing actions and improving behavior while accounting for stochastic transitions.
icml-2005-reinforcement-learning-with-ga.tldr: The paper extends Gaussian-process value learning to stochastic transitions and introduces GPSARSA for action selection and policy improvement.

paragraphs: The paper studies supervised clustering: learning how to group future sets of items from examples of complete clusterings. The training information describes how entire sets should be partitioned. Applications include grouping noun phrases that refer to the same entity and grouping news articles that concern the same topic.

The proposed support-vector-machine algorithm trains a clustering procedure by adapting its measure of similarity between pairs of items. This makes the pairwise similarity a learned component of the overall grouping process. The approach can optimize a variety of clustering functions against a variety of clustering performance measures, allowing training to reflect different definitions of a desirable clustering.

The authors evaluate the algorithm empirically on noun-phrase clustering and news-article clustering. These applications connect the training formulation to two stated uses of supervised grouping. The central contribution is a way to learn the similarity measure from complete clustering examples while accommodating different clustering procedures and evaluation objectives within the proposed SVM-based approach.
icml-2005-supervised-clustering-with-sup.tldr: An SVM learns pairwise similarity from example clusterings to train clustering algorithms for future item sets.

paragraphs: The paper evaluates a technique for improving Bayesian inference in classification and regression tree models. Full Bayesian inference requires a posterior distribution over all possible trees. Because exact computation is not possible for this task, the approach uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to approximate that distribution.

The difficulty is that the posterior contains many local modes, or regions of relatively high posterior probability. A Markov chain can become stuck in one such region, limiting its exploration of the possible trees. Tempering is introduced to counter this behavior, with the aim of helping the chain move beyond the local modes that impede inference.

The authors experimentally assess tempering and report a clear improvement. The result supports its use as a technique for improving the approximate Bayesian computation in these tree models. The paper’s focus is the quality of the inference process: it tackles the difficulty of exploring a complicated posterior, which is necessary for representing the range of possible trees under the Bayesian formulation.
icml-2005-tempering-for-bayesian-c-rt-a4.tldr: Tempering improves approximate Bayesian inference for tree models by helping MCMC avoid becoming trapped in local posterior modes.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian framework for hidden Markov random fields, a class of graphical models suited to image modeling. It applies the framework to image segmentation. The main computational obstacle is that exact inference in these models is intractable, making both training and use difficult.

The authors introduce an efficient variational method for approximate inference in the Bayesian formulation. This approximation supports density estimation and model selection as well as inference. These tasks are connected: learning an image model requires estimating its probabilistic behavior and choosing a suitable model, while segmentation uses the learned representation.

Experiments on real-world images show the proposed technique outperforming recent segmentation methods based on hidden Markov random fields. The result supports the practical value of the variational treatment for the evaluated segmentation problems. The contribution is both computational and methodological: approximate Bayesian inference makes a difficult model family more usable and provides a shared framework for several tasks involved in learning image models.
icml-2005-variational-bayesian-image-mod.tldr: Efficient variational Bayesian inference makes hidden Markov random fields usable for image modeling and improves segmentation in the reported experiments.
